title: Man page questions
about: Questions you can answer with the manual pages installed in the lab: the terminal is open beside each one, so look it up (`man`, `help`, `whatis`, `apropos`) instead of guessing. Choices, fill in the blank, ordering, matching and sorting.

questions.title: The parts of a man page
questions.text: Open `man find` and look at the headings in capitals. Pair each part with what you find in it.

pairs.r: the command and a one-line description
the ways of calling the command
pairs.why: Square brackets mean optional; read it before the options.

pairs.r: what the command does, with the list of its options
pairs.why: In some pages the options have their own OPTIONS heading.

pairs.r: ready-to-copy command lines
pairs.why: Not every page has this part: look for it at the end.

pairs.r: what the exit codes mean
related commands and pages
pairs.why: A good way to find the command you were really looking for.

questions.title: Reading a SYNOPSIS
questions.text: `man cut` shows `cut OPTION... [FILE]...`. What does it say?

options.t: You can give any number of options, and any number of files, including none.
options.why: Square brackets mean optional and the dots mean "and more of the same".

options.t: `OPTION` and `FILE` are literal words that you must type.
options.why: Words in capitals are placeholders: you replace them with a real option or file name.

options.t: You must give exactly one file, and the options are optional.
options.why: `[FILE]...` allows several files or none (then `cut` reads the standard input).

options.t: You can give options only after the files.
options.why: The synopsis lists the options first, and GNU commands accept them there.

questions.title: Which call fits the SYNOPSIS?
questions.text: In `man cp` the synopsis has `cp [OPTION]... SOURCE... DIRECTORY`. Which of these calls fits it?

options.why: Two sources, and the last argument is the destination directory.
It has a destination but no source to copy.
It has a source but no destination: the last argument is always the target.
The brackets in the manual only show that something is optional: you do not type them.

questions.title: Short and long options
questions.text: `man head` lists `-n, --lines=[-]NUM`. Which call prints the first 5 lines of `datos.txt` using the **long** form?

options.why: Long options start with two hyphens and take their value after `=`.
Two hyphens go with the long name (`--lines`), not with the letter.
A single hyphen introduces letters: this would be read as the options `-l -i -n -e -s`.
The short option takes its value as the next word (`-n 5`), without `=`.

questions.title: Look up an option
questions.text: You need the option of `grep` that prints only the matching part of a line. Put the steps in a sensible order.

items.why: The page opens in the pager.
The pager jumps to the first place where the word appears.

items.t: Press `n` until the highlighted text is the description of the option itself (`-o, --only-matching`)
items.why: The first match may be a mention elsewhere; `n` moves to the next one.
Leave the page and try the option in the terminal.

questions.title: Keys inside a man page
questions.text: `man` shows its pages with the pager `less`. Press `h` inside one to see its keys, then pair each key with what it does.

pairs.r: searches forward for `word`
pairs.why: The slash starts a search; matches are highlighted.

pairs.r: jumps to the next match of the last search
goes back to the top of the page
pairs.why: Handy after jumping around with searches.

pairs.r: goes to the end of the page
pairs.why: The last lines are often the SEE ALSO and examples.

pairs.r: leaves the page
pairs.why: It returns to the shell prompt.

extras.why: `less` has no such key: redirect the output of `man` yourself if you want a copy.

questions.title: Which page describes /etc/passwd?
questions.text: You want the **layout of the fields of the file `/etc/passwd`**, not the `passwd` command that changes a password. Which command opens that page? Try them in the terminal.
questions.note: `whatis passwd` lists every section that has a page with that name, and `man -k passwd` lists every page that mentions it.

options.why: Section 5 holds file formats and configuration files. `passwd (5)` is the page about the file.
It opens the first page called `passwd`, which is the command (section 1), not the file format.
Section 1 is for commands: this is the same page as plain `man passwd`.
There is no page named `etc`; the page is named after the file, `passwd`, and the number only picks the section.

questions.title: List the pages about a word
questions.text: To list every manual entry whose one-line description mentions a word, type `{{0}} word`.
questions.note: `apropos` and `man -k` are the same search. When you do not know the name of the command, describe it: `apropos 'list directory'`.

wrong.why: `whatis` looks a name up and prints its own one-line description; it does not search the descriptions for a word.
`man -f` is the same as `whatis`: it matches the name of a page.

questions.title: A one-line description
questions.text: You see `tar` in a script and want one line telling what it is. Which command prints exactly that?

options.why: It prints the NAME line of the page: command and short description.
Alone it needs a keyword; with one, it lists every page that mentions it, not only `tar`.
It tells where the shell finds `tar` (a file path), not what it does.
That is an operation of `tar` itself (list an archive), not a description.

questions.title: help or man?
questions.text: Bash builtins are documented with `help`, external programs with `man`. Check with `type NAME` in the terminal, then put each command in the right group.

items.why: `type cd` says it is a shell builtin: it must change the directory of the shell itself.
A builtin of bash. Careful: `man read` opens a different page (the POSIX utility, or the system call), not bash's `read`.
A builtin: it works on the positional parameters of the running shell.
A builtin: it changes the environment of the shell.
A program in `/usr/bin`: its page is `man find`.
A program in `/usr/bin`.
A program in `/usr/bin`.
A program in `/usr/bin`.

questions.title: ls options
questions.text: Pair each option of `ls` with its effect (`man ls`).

pairs.r: shows the hidden entries (names starting with a dot)
long listing: type and permissions, links, owner, group, size and date
pairs.why: The format you read permissions from.

pairs.r: lists a directory itself, not its contents
lists subdirectories recursively
pairs.why: Every directory gets its own heading.

pairs.r: prints the inode number of each entry
pairs.why: Two names of the same file (hard links) share the number.

pairs.r: sorts by modification time, newest first

questions.title: Options of cp
questions.text: Pair each option of `cp` (`man cp`) with its effect.

pairs.r: copies directories and everything inside them
keeps the permissions, owner and modification times
does not overwrite an existing file
pairs.why: Nothing is replaced, and no error is raised.

pairs.r: asks before overwriting
pairs.why: Interactive: a script would wait for an answer.

pairs.r: copies only when the source is newer than the destination (or missing)
explains what is being done

questions.title: rm, mv and mkdir
questions.text: Pair each command line with its effect.

pairs.r: removes the directory and everything inside it
pairs.why: `rmdir dir` only works when it is empty.

pairs.r: asks before removing
pairs.why: A safety net when you type by hand.

pairs.r: never asks, and does not complain if the file does not exist
does not overwrite `b` if it exists
creates the missing parents, and no error if it exists
creates `d` with the permissions 700
pairs.why: The mode is given as an octal number.

questions.title: One line with the total
questions.text: To print only the **total size** of the directory `fotos`, in human-readable units (like `4.2M`), type `du -{{0}} fotos`.
questions.note: `-s` is `--summarize` and `-h` is `--human-readable`; `du -h --max-depth=1` shows one line per subdirectory instead.

wrong.why: `-a` lists every file, not just a total.
`-c` adds a grand total line after the listing, but the listing is still there.

questions.title: Two kinds of link
questions.text: You run `ln notas.txt a` and `ln -s notas.txt b`, and then delete `notas.txt`. What happens (`man ln`)?

options.t: `a` still shows the content and `b` is a broken link.
options.why: `a` is another name of the same inode (a hard link); `b` only stores the path `notas.txt`, which no longer exists.

options.t: Both `a` and `b` still show the content.
options.why: A symbolic link stores a path: once the target is gone it points to nothing.

options.t: `a` is broken and `b` still shows the content.
options.why: It is the other way round: the hard link shares the inode, the symbolic one depends on the name.

options.t: Both are broken, because deleting a file removes its links.
options.why: The data survives while at least one name (hard link) still points to the inode.

questions.title: Name without directory and extension
questions.text: In a script, `f=/home/ana/informes/mayo.txt`. Which command prints just `mayo` (`man basename`)?

options.why: `basename NAME SUFFIX` removes the leading directories and the trailing suffix.
`dirname` prints the directory part (`/home/ana/informes`) and takes no suffix.
The suffix goes last; this prints `.txt` with `$f` taken as the suffix.
There is no `-d` that strips the extension; the suffix is given as an argument.

questions.title: Tests of find
questions.text: Pair each test of `find` with what it selects (`man find`).

pairs.r: regular files only
pairs.why: `-type d` is for directories and `-type l` for symbolic links.

pairs.r: names that match the pattern (case matters)
files bigger than 10 mebibytes
files owned by the user `ana`
pairs.why: `-group` does the same for the group.

pairs.r: empty files and empty directories
pairs.why: Often combined with `-type f` or `-type d`.

extras.why: It is an action, not a test: it selects nothing.

questions.title: The three forms of -perm
questions.text: Read the `-perm` entries of `man find` and pair each test with what it selects.

pairs.r: files whose permissions are exactly 644
files that have at least those bits set (they may have more)
pairs.why: The minus sign: all the listed bits are set.

pairs.r: files that have any of the execute bits set
pairs.why: The slash: at least one of the listed bits.

pairs.r: files the owner can execute
pairs.why: Symbolic modes work with the minus form too.

questions.title: Time and size tests
questions.text: Pair each test of `find` (`man find`) with what it selects.

pairs.r: modified more than 7 days ago
pairs.why: `+` means more than, `-` means less than.

pairs.r: modified less than a day ago
pairs.why: That is, in the last 24 hours.

pairs.r: modified in the last 30 minutes
pairs.why: The same idea, counted in minutes.

pairs.r: modified more recently than the file `ref`
pairs.why: Compares with another file instead of a number.

pairs.r: bigger than 1 mebibyte

questions.title: Tests or actions
questions.text: In a `find` command line, **tests** select files and **actions** do something with the selected ones. Sort the expressions (the EXPRESSION part of `man find`).

items.why: Matches the file name against a pattern.
Matches the kind of file: `f`, `d`, `l`...
Matches the permission bits.
Matches the time of the last modification, counted in days.
Prints the name: it is the default action when you give none.
Removes the file. Put it last, after every test.
Runs a command for the selected files.

questions.title: The braces in -exec
questions.text: In `find . -name '*.tmp' -exec rm {} \;`, what do the braces `{}` stand for?

options.t: Each file that `find` found, one at a time.
options.why: `find` replaces `{}` with the name before running the command.
That is the first argument of `find` (`.`), not the braces.

options.t: All the file names at once, as a single list.
options.why: With `\;` the command runs once for each file; only the `+` form groups them.

options.t: The output of the previous command in the pipe.
options.why: `{}` has nothing to do with pipes.

questions.title: Delete with care
questions.text: You must delete the empty `.tmp` files below `work/`. Put the steps in the order a careful person would follow.

items.t: Run `find work -type f -name '*.tmp' -empty` and read the list
items.why: First see what the tests select, with the default action `-print`.

items.t: Check that no wanted file is in the list
items.why: Fix the tests if it is: it is cheaper than restoring files.

items.t: Run the same command with `-delete` added **at the end**
items.why: `-delete` after the tests: put first, it would apply to everything `find` visits.

items.t: Run the first command again and check that the list is now empty
items.why: Proves the files are gone and nothing else broke.

questions.title: grep options
questions.text: Pair each option of `grep` with its effect (`man grep`).

pairs.r: ignores upper/lower case
prints the lines that do **not** match
prints only the number of matching lines
pairs.why: Not the number of matches: a line counts once.

pairs.r: prints only the part of the line that matches
prints only the names of the files that contain a match
pairs.why: `-L` prints the ones that do not.

pairs.r: matches whole words only

questions.title: Extended regular expressions
questions.text: Which option of `grep` lets you write `error|warning` or `ab+` in the pattern without backslashes (`man grep`)?

options.why: `--extended-regexp`: the pattern is an extended regular expression (alternation, `+`, `?`, `{}`, `()`).
`--fixed-strings`: the pattern is taken literally, with no special characters at all.
It only marks the next argument as a pattern (useful for patterns that start with `-`).
It prints only the matching part of each line; it does not change how the pattern is read.

questions.title: Options of cut
questions.text: Pair each way of calling `cut` (`man cut`) with what it prints.

pairs.r: the first field, using `:` as the separator
the 2nd and the 4th fields of a CSV
from the 3rd field to the last one
the first five characters of each line

questions.title: Sort by a column
questions.text: A file has lines like `ana:35:madrid`. To sort them by the **2nd field**, **numerically**, type `sort -t{{0}} -k{{1}} -n file`.
questions.note: `-t` sets the field separator and `-k` the sort key (field number); `-n` compares as numbers, so `9` comes before `10`.

wrong.why: `-k1` would sort by the name, the first field.
The fields are separated by `:`, so `-t,` would treat each line as one single field.

questions.title: sort and uniq options
questions.text: Pair each command with its effect (`man sort`, `man uniq`).

pairs.r: compares as numbers, so 9 comes before 10
reverses the order
keeps only one copy of repeated lines
sorts by the 2nd field instead of the whole line
pairs.why: Fields are separated by blanks unless `-t` says otherwise.

pairs.r: prefixes each line with the number of times it repeats
prints only the lines that are repeated
pairs.why: Again, repeated lines must be adjacent.

questions.title: Why uniq is not enough
questions.text: `uniq names.txt` leaves duplicates in the output of an unsorted file. Why (`man uniq`)?

options.t: It only compares **adjacent** lines, so the file must be sorted first (`sort names.txt | uniq`).
options.why: The first line of the page says it: "Filter adjacent matching lines".

options.t: It only compares the first word of each line, so use `-f` to compare all of it.
options.why: It compares the whole line unless you ask otherwise with `-f`, `-s` or `-w`.

options.t: It removes duplicates only when `-u` is given, because by default it just counts them.
options.why: Without options it already prints each group of identical adjacent lines once; `-c` counts, `-u` keeps the unique ones.

options.t: It only works on files with at most 100 lines.
options.why: There is no such limit.

questions.title: head, tail and wc
questions.text: Pair each command with what it prints.

pairs.r: the first 5 lines
the last 5 lines
everything from line 5 to the end
pairs.why: With a plus sign the number is where to start.

pairs.r: the number of lines (and the file name)
pairs.why: With `< f` only the number is printed.

pairs.r: the number of words

questions.title: Options of tr
questions.text: `tr` translates characters. Which of these are options of `tr`? Check `man tr`.

options.why: Deletes the characters of SET1.
Squeezes runs of a repeated character into one.
Complements SET1: acts on everything that is **not** in it.
There is no `-r` option in `tr`.
There is no `-l` option; lines are not a concept `tr` knows.

questions.title: tar options
questions.text: Pair each option of `tar` with what it does (`man tar`).

pairs.r: creates a new archive
pairs.why: One of the three main operations.

pairs.r: extracts files from an archive
pairs.why: Into the current directory unless you add `-C`.

pairs.r: lists the contents of an archive
filters the archive through gzip
says which archive file to use
pairs.why: It must be followed by the file name, so it goes last in `-czf name`.

pairs.r: changes to `dir` before doing the operation

questions.title: One file out of a .tgz
questions.text: You need only `docs/report.txt` out of `backup.tgz`, without extracting everything. Put the steps in order.

items.why: List the archive to learn the exact name of the member.

items.t: Find `docs/report.txt` in the list and copy the name exactly
items.why: The name must match what is stored, including the directory.
Extract only that member, creating `docs/` as needed.
Check that it is there.

questions.title: chmod, symbolic modes
questions.text: Pair each symbolic mode (`man chmod`) with what it does.

pairs.r: adds execute permission for the owner
removes write permission from group and others
lets everybody read it
leaves others with no permissions at all
pairs.why: `=` sets exactly the listed bits (none here).

pairs.r: sets the permissions to 755

questions.title: Octal and symbolic
questions.text: Pair each octal mode with its symbolic form.

pairs.r: `rwxr-xr-x`
pairs.why: 7 = rwx for the owner, 5 = r-x for group and others.
Only the owner can do anything.
Everyone can read, nobody can write.

pairs.r: `rw-rw-r--`
pairs.why: Typical for a file shared by a group.

questions.title: New files and the umask
questions.text: With `umask 027`, a **new regular file** that the program asked to create with mode 666 gets the permissions `{{0}}` (in octal).
questions.note: `help umask` explains the mask: the permissions requested (666 for files, 777 for directories) minus the bits of the mask: 666 - 027 = 640.

wrong.why: That is what a new **directory** (asked with 777) gets: files never start with the execute bit.
`027` is the mask itself: the bits that are taken away.

questions.title: Owner and group at once
questions.text: Which command changes **both the owner and the group** of `data.txt` to `ana` and `dev` (`man chown`)? Changing the owner needs root, so only read the page.

options.why: `OWNER:GROUP` sets both in one go.
It would treat `dev` as a second file name.
A leading colon means "only the group", and the name would be wrong anyway.
`chmod` changes permission bits, not owners.

questions.title: Operators of test
questions.text: Pair each operator of `[ ... ]` (`man test`) with what it checks.

pairs.r: FILE exists (of any type)
FILE exists and is a regular file
FILE exists and is a directory
FILE exists and has a size greater than zero
FILE1 is newer than FILE2
the length of STRING is zero

questions.title: Smaller than, as a number
questions.text: Inside `[ ... ]`, which expression is true when the **number** in `$n` is smaller than 10?

options.why: `-lt` compares integers: less than.
`<` is an **input redirection** for the shell: it would try to read from a file named `10`.
`=` compares strings for equality.
`-le` is less **or equal**: it is also true when `$n` is 10.

questions.title: Asking the user
questions.text: To show the text `Name: ` before reading a line into the variable `name`, type `read -{{0}} "Name: " name`. Look at `help read`.
questions.note: `-p` prints the prompt without a final newline. `-r` (do not treat backslashes specially) is a good habit when reading lines of text.

wrong.why: `-a` stores the words in an array instead.

questions.title: Where is ${var:-default}?
questions.text: You remember `${var:-default}` and want its exact rule. In which section of `man bash` do you find it? Search for it in the pager.

options.why: It lists `${parameter:-word}`, `${parameter:=word}`, `${parameter#word}`... with their rules.
That section is about patterns such as `*` and `?` in file names.
That section is about `$(...)` and the backquote form.
It documents builtins like `read` and `test`, not the expansion syntax.

questions.title: Special parameters
questions.text: Pair each special parameter of the shell with what it holds (`man bash`, the Special Parameters part).

pairs.r: the number of arguments the script received
the exit status of the last command
the name of the script
all the arguments, each one as a separate word (in double quotes)
pairs.why: `for a in "$@"` visits every argument whole.

pairs.r: the process ID of the shell

questions.title: Redirection operators
questions.text: Pair each operator with what it does (`man bash`, the REDIRECTION part).

pairs.r: writes the output to the file, replacing its content
pairs.why: The file is created or emptied first.

pairs.r: appends the output to the end of the file
pairs.why: The file is created if it does not exist.

pairs.r: sends the error messages to the file
reads the input from the file
feeds the output of the first as the input of the second
pairs.why: A pipe: both run at once.

pairs.r: sends both the output and the errors to the file
pairs.why: The order of the operators matters.

questions.title: Fields of /etc/passwd
questions.text: Each line of `/etc/passwd` has `{{0}}` fields separated by colons (see `man 5 passwd`).
questions.note: Login name, password (`x`), UID, GID, comment, home directory and shell.

wrong.why: Count again: name, password, UID, GID, comment, home and shell.
The comment (GECOS) field and the shell are also fields.

questions.title: What each field is
questions.text: Pair the fields of `/etc/passwd` with their meaning (`man 5 passwd`).

pairs.r: the login name
pairs.why: What you type to log in.

pairs.r: the numeric user ID
the numeric group ID
the home directory
the login shell

questions.title: A ! in /etc/shadow
questions.text: In `/etc/shadow`, the second field of a user is `!` (or `*`). What does it mean (`man 5 shadow`)?

options.t: The account has no valid password: nobody can log in with a password as that user.
options.why: A string that is not a valid result of `crypt(3)` can never match what is typed.

options.t: The user has an empty password, so anyone can log in without typing one.
options.why: An empty field would mean that; `!` blocks the password login.

options.t: The password has expired and must be changed at the next login.
options.why: Expiry is controlled by other fields (the dates), not by this one.
Nothing in this file marks administrators; that is done by groups and `sudoers`.

questions.title: Reading a crontab line
questions.text: When does `30 2 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/backup` run (`man 5 crontab`)?

options.why: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week: minute 30, hour 2, any day, any month, weekday 1 (Monday).

options.t: Every 30 minutes between 2 and 3 in the morning on the first day of the month.
options.why: A `1` in the 5th field is a weekday; and `30` is a fixed minute, not a step.

options.t: At 02:30 on the first day of every month.
options.why: The first day of the month would be a `1` in the **third** field; here it is in the fifth.

options.t: At 01:02 on the 30th of every month.
options.why: The order of the fields is minute, hour, day: the first field is minutes.

questions.title: Fields of a crontab line
questions.text: Put the five time fields of a crontab line in their order, from left to right.

items.why: 0-7, where both 0 and 7 are Sunday.

questions.title: The NOPASSWD tag
questions.text: In `/etc/sudoers`, the line `ana ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` allows... (`man 5 sudoers`, look up the tag)

options.t: `ana` to run any command as any user via `sudo`, with no password prompt.
options.why: `NOPASSWD:` is a tag of the command list: the password prompt is skipped for those commands.

options.t: every user of the system to run any command as `ana`, without a password prompt.
options.why: The first field is **who** may use sudo: here it is `ana`, not "anybody".

options.t: `ana` to log in to the machine without typing a password at the login prompt.
options.why: It concerns `sudo` only; login passwords are not part of `sudoers`.

options.t: `ana` to run only one program, whose file is literally called `ALL`, with a password.
options.why: `ALL` is a keyword that matches every command.

questions.title: ps options
questions.text: Pair each way of calling `ps` with what it shows (`man ps`).

pairs.r: every process of the system
a full-format listing (UID, PID, PPID, start time...)
every process, in full format
pairs.why: The most common way to look for a process.

pairs.r: every process of every user, with the owner and the CPU and memory use
the processes of the user ana
pairs.why: By effective user ID or name.

pairs.r: the process with PID 1234
pairs.why: A list of PIDs is accepted.

questions.title: From a signal number to its name
questions.text: A log says a process died from **signal 11**. Which command tells you the **name** of signal 11 (look at the EXAMPLES of `man kill`)?

options.why: `-l` (`--list`) with a number converts it to the name (`SEGV`); with a name it gives the number.
It is the way to **send** signal 11, and it needs a PID to send it to.
`-s` also sends the signal: it expects a PID after it.
`-q` sends a signal together with an integer value (`sigqueue`): it does not translate anything.

questions.title: Signal numbers
questions.text: The signal that `kill` sends by default, `TERM`, has the number {{0}}. Check it with `kill -l TERM`.
questions.note: `kill -l 15` prints `TERM` and `kill -l TERM` prints `15`: the option converts in both directions.

wrong.why: 9 is `KILL`, the one that cannot be caught.

questions.title: The groups of a user
questions.text: Which command prints the **names** (not the numbers) of **all the groups** of the user `ana` (`man id`)?

options.why: `-G` prints all group IDs and `-n` asks for names instead of numbers.
`-g` prints only the primary group.
`-u` is the user, not the groups.
It prints the numbers of all the groups, because `-n` is missing.

questions.title: who or last?
questions.text: `who` reports the **current** state of the system and `last` reads the **history** of logins. Check `man who` and `man last`, then sort the facts.

items.t: Who is logged in right now, and from which terminal
items.why: The default output of `who`.

items.t: The time of the last system boot, with `-b`
items.why: `who -b`.

items.t: Every past login of every user, newest first
items.why: `last` reads the history file `/var/log/wtmp`.

items.t: The list of reboots, with `last reboot`
items.why: `reboot` works as a pseudo user that logs in at every boot.

questions.title: To the background
questions.text: You started `sleep 300` in the foreground and pressed `Ctrl+Z`, which **suspended** it. Which command now lets it **continue running in the background**? (`help bg`)

options.why: It resumes the suspended job in the background.
It resumes the job in the **foreground**: the shell waits for it again.
It only lists the jobs and their state.
It waits until the background jobs end: it does not resume a stopped one.

questions.title: systemctl
questions.text: Pair each `systemctl` command with its effect on a service such as `ssh` (`man systemctl`).

pairs.r: starts it now
pairs.why: It does not change what happens at the next boot.

pairs.r: stops it now
pairs.why: The service stays enabled for the next boot.

pairs.r: stops it and starts it again
makes it start automatically at boot
pairs.why: It does not start it now (unless you add `--now`).

pairs.r: shows whether it is running, with its latest log lines
